name: Heartland Beef
blurb: One big packing plant in Prairie Bend, 1,400 line workers, and about 600 ranches that sell it cattle. Founder Walt Dreyer started as a rancher and holds 28% of the vote.

directors.name: Carla Whitfield
directors.title: Attorney
directors.motive: You are outside counsel and have seen the complaint numbers. You know that calling it a few bad employees is the line a regulator will examine, and you want your advice in writing. Heartland is your firm's biggest client, and your partners would rather you not become a witness.

directors.name: Denise Kowalski
directors.title: Labor director
directors.motive: You speak for the plant workers, and some of your members' cousins are the field staff who were fired. You think the people at the bottom took the blame for targets set at the top, but if the stock falls and the plant loses cattle, your members lose hours.

directors.name: Marcus Feld
directors.title: Fund partner
directors.motive: Your fund owns 9% and you told your investors the program count was why you bought. A drop in a headline metric can hurt the price, and a fraud story can wipe out a company. You do not want to learn which one this is from a newspaper.

directors.name: Gus Halvorsen
directors.title: Founder's friend
directors.home: Walt Dreyer, the founder (hunting partner of 30 years)
directors.motive: Walt Dreyer is your hunting partner of thirty years, proud of the culture he thinks the count measures, and he will not believe the stories without proof. He is more worried about Karen Mueller than he admits, and a vote against her could end your hunting weekends.

directors.name: Luanne Pruitt
directors.title: Community seat
directors.motive: You lead the co-op whose members found fees on their checks, and you were elected to protect them. Heartland is also the only buyer within a day's haul for many ranchers, your own herd included. You want an apology and a refund, and you need the plant to stay open.

directors.name: Howard Lindqvist
directors.title: Audit chair
directors.motive: You signed the last three audits, and the program count was a figure you reviewed. Calling this a few bad employees protects your record, while calling it a design flaw means you missed it. You want a review that finds a process failure, not a person, and not you.

briefing.intro: Heartland Beef runs one packing plant with 1,400 line workers and about 600 supplier ranches. Founder Walt Dreyer holds 28% of the vote, and the annual shareholder meeting is in five weeks.
facts: Reps are paid a bonus for each program a rancher or grocer joins, under the slogan five programs per account. The average has risen from 2.1 to 4.6, and analysts and lenders treat it as proof of customer loyalty.

A newspaper plans a story in ten days about reps who enrolled ranchers in fee-charging programs without their knowledge. The ethics hotline logged 650 enrollment complaints in two years, and 230 field staff were fired, mostly at the lowest levels.
Karen Mueller runs the sales division, which brings in 60% of profit. She calls it a handful of cheaters and says the targets are fair, and her own bonus rides on the count.

Dropping the targets could cut the program count by half in two years and the stock ($52) by 15% or more. Keeping them risks fines and lawsuits, and regulators have been gentler with firms that changed course before the story ran.
Improper fees are estimated at $4 million to $40 million. Ranchers are angry, and a boycott by a quarter of them would leave the plant short of cattle.

options.title: End the targets
options.text: Drop the bonus, refund every disputed fee, and have an outside firm review all enrollments.

options.title: Keep the targets and police them
options.text: Keep the bonus, add confirmation calls to ranchers, and fire anyone caught.

options.title: Review before deciding
options.text: Change nothing now, hire an outside firm to report in six months, and say we take it seriously.

options.title: Change the people
options.text: Move Karen Mueller out of sales and let an interim head decide on the targets later.

reveal.text: The real firm was Wells Fargo, whose goal was eight products per household. Employees opened accounts customers had not asked for, regulators fined the bank $185 million in 2016, and about 5,300 employees were fired. The directors' later report found the board's information was incomplete. CEO John Stumpf left and the sales goals were dropped.

questions: Why pay reps per program signed?
Heartland fired 230 staff. Why didn't that fix it?
You're Walt's friend. Do you vote against Karen?

press.headline: Heartland Beef Ends Sales Targets and Refunds Ranchers
press.story: The company dropped its five-programs bonus and will refund every disputed fee after an outside review. Analysts cut growth forecasts, and ranchers called the apology overdue but welcome.

press.headline: Heartland Beef Adds Confirmation Calls, Keeps Sales Bonus
press.story: Reps will phone ranchers to confirm each sign-up, and anyone caught will be fired. The ranchers' co-op says firing more low-level staff misses the people who set the targets.

press.headline: Heartland Beef Orders Six-Month Review of Sales Plan
press.story: The company says it takes the matter seriously but changes nothing now. The newspaper ran its story on schedule, and a state regulator has asked for the standard rancher contract.

press.headline: Heartland Beef Moves Top Sales Executive Out
press.story: Karen Mueller leaves the division, and an interim head will decide on targets after ninety days. Analysts noted the division brings in 60% of profit and asked who will hold the numbers.
